title: Aryna Sabalenka and Iga Świątek withdraw from Dubai WTA 1000 tournament
content:
The top two players in the world, Aryna Sabalenka and Iga Świątek, have followed through on their promises to play a lighter schedule this year as early as February. Both of them have withdrawn from next week’s Dubai Tennis Championships, a mandatory WTA 1000 event one rung below the Grand Slams.

Neither player cited a specific injury in their statements confirming their withdrawal on Friday, and a spokesperson for Świątek said via text message that she’s feeling well and will be preparing for next month’s BNP Paribas Open in Indian Wells, Calif.

A spokesperson for Sabalenka was not immediately available for comment.

In a statement from the tournament, Sabalenka said that she was “not feeling 100 percent,” while Świątek said that her decision was “due to a change of schedule.”

It’s the latest example of players taking their scheduling into their own hands and accepting the rankings points and financial penalties that come with missing an event of this size. Highly ranked players like Sabalenka and Świątek are required to play in the four Grand Slams, 10 WTA 1000 tournaments and six WTA 500 events under the association’s rules. The former called this schedule “insane” last month, the latter “a madness” in September.

Both were deducted ranking points last year, and in 2024, for failing to play enough 500-level events, while Sabalenka also missed this week’s Qatar Open, another WTA 1000 in which Świątek lost in the quarterfinals to Greece’s Maria Sakkari.

After losing to Elena Rybakina at the Australian Open last month, Świątek said that she would “for sure” skip some mandatory 1000 events this year, as it was the only way for her to work on her game, especially her serve. “Last year I had trouble with making this kind of decision, but this year I’m trying to change my approach,” she said in a news conference. “So I think, for sure, we’ll skip some 1000 tournaments.”

And she has long been a critic of the WTA’s schedule and number of mandatory events, calling the situation “a madness” during the China Open last September on a day when five of the 12 matches at the combined men’s and women’s event ended in mid-match retirements.

“Perhaps I’ll have to choose some tournaments and skip them, even if they are mandatory,” Świątek said in a news conference. “The WTA has made this a madness with all these mandatory rules.

“It’s impossible to fit everything in the calendar. I don’t think any elite player can manage it.”

The WTA said in a statement at the time that “athlete welfare is always a top priority,” and emphasized the $400 million increase in player compensation that the rules on mandatory events, implemented in 2024, have underpinned.

Sabalenka, meanwhile, said during her Brisbane International title run in January that playing as light a schedule as Serena Williams did in her heyday had become impossible.

“The season is definitely insane, and that’s not good for all of us, as you see so many players getting injured and also the balls are quite heavy. It’s a lot of struggle for all of us,” Sabalenka said in a news conference.

“The rules are quite tricky with mandatory events, but I’m still skipping a couple events to protect my body, because I struggled a lot last season. Even though the results were really consistent, some of the tournaments I had been playing completely sick or I’ve been really exhausted from overplaying.

“This season we will try to manage it a little bit better, even though they are going to fine me by the end of the season. But it’s tricky to do that. You cannot skip a 1000 event. It’s really tricky, and I think that’s insane what they do. I think they just follow their interests, but they’re not focusing on protecting all of us.”

A WTA spokesperson said in response that “athlete welfare is, and will always remain, a top priority for the WTA. We listen and engage closely with players on all matters relating to the tennis season, including through the WTA Players’ Council and player representatives on the WTA Board.

“We are committed to supporting athlete welfare and sustaining the long-term health of the sport. Based on feedback from our players, tournaments, and fans, we continue to review and explore improvements to our Tour structure, working in coordination with the ATP, ITF and Grand Slams.”

On the men’s side, there have been similar complaints, with world No. 1 Carlos Alcaraz saying in September 2024 that tennis’ schedule meant that “probably they are going to kill us in some way.” He and world No. 2 Jannik Sinner both skipped the Canadian Open (a mandatory 1000 event) last year and play a lighter schedule than most, but very few players can afford to lose the ranking points and money on offer at the big events.

When Alexander Zverev, the world No. 4, was asked at the Australian Open if he would consider a similar strategy to the top two, he replied: “Yeah, but they’re making $50 million a year. We’re not all Carlos and Jannik.”

The fear is that, in tennis terms, the rich get richer because only the most privileged can afford to take off the time to recharge and work on one’s game that the mandatory rules, if followed, don’t allow.

Sabalenka, like Świątek, is expected to return in Indian Wells, which gets underway Wednesday March 4. Sabalenka lost to Mirra Andreeva in last year’s final.
